title: Processing-plant wet cleaning: dry removal, drains and protein-safe rinsing
audience: Cleaners and supervisors working in food-processing, food-storage or food-service areas under a site sanitation plan.
learningOutcomes: Remove dry debris by hand tools before any water is applied to a food-processing surface.
Explain why a hot rinse or steam can set protein soil onto equipment.
Clear floor drains and channels during the wet clean, then record the result.
Keep water away from electrical equipment, motors and dry stored goods during a wet clean.

instruction.heading: Dry removal comes before any water
instruction.body: In a processing area the first job is to take away solid material by hand. A shovel, scraper or squeegee moves trim, shell, vegetable matter and similar debris into a container or onto a conveyor that carries it out of the building. A hose is the wrong first tool here, because it pushes solids into drains, under equipment and toward product. In a food-service kitchen the same logic applies on a smaller scale: a dustpan with a long handle collects solids and paper, and a damp cloth or mop contains spilled liquid. Dry sweeping is avoided wherever food is exposed, because it lifts particles into the air where they can settle on food or work surfaces.

instruction.heading: Rinse with cool or lukewarm water
instruction.body: Once the solids are gone, a rinse lifts the fine residue left by seafood, red meat, poultry, produce, dairy or egg material. Cool or lukewarm water works best. Hot water and steam can bake protein onto a surface, the way an egg fixes itself to a dry pan. Proteins set when they are heated, so a rinse that is too hot makes the next step harder and leaves the surface less clean. Keep water and spray away from motors, control panels and electrical units. Where belts are lifted on metal bars for cleaning, remove the bars before the equipment runs again, or the belt and equipment can be damaged. Disassemble parts such as band saws, pipes and stuffers so the rinse reaches the surfaces underneath.

instruction.heading: Drains, coolers and moisture in storage
instruction.body: Floor drains and channels belong to the clean, not to a separate task. A drain that holds old food debris becomes a source of odour and a place where microorganisms and pests can build up, so it is cleared and flushed during every wet clean. Coolers that hold wet product, such as seafood, red meat, poultry, dairy or produce, need regular cleaning too. Keep water out of dry goods stores: moisture that carries into a dry store can damage packaging and product. The supervisor of the wet clean should check the drains, the cooler floors and any area that is often overlooked, and record that the check was made.

procedure: Confirm the zone, the equipment and whether the task is a routine clean or an authorised sanitising task.
Remove all solid debris by shovel, scraper, broom or squeegee, and place it in covered containers or on the waste conveyor.
Protect electrical equipment, motors and dry goods before any water is used.
Rinse the surfaces with cool or lukewarm water, working from the highest point toward the drains.
Disassemble any parts that cannot be rinsed in place, and rinse them separately.
Clear and flush the floor drains and channels, and check that water flows freely.
Record the zone, the times, the drain check and any part that could not be cleaned, then pass the zone on to sanitising.

workedExamples.situation: A meat-trim line ends its shift. Trim and bone pieces lie under the conveyor and along the base of the machine. The team clears the solids into a covered bin and moves it off the line before any water is used.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: A colleague suggests a fast hot-water hose-down to save time. What should happen instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The team keeps the dry removal first, uses cool water, keeps spray away from the motor and clears the drain. The record shows the zone was dry-cleared, rinsed and drained.

equipmentAndPpe: Shovel and scraper suited to the surface
Waterproof apron, boots with slip-resistant soles, and gloves
Eye protection wherever water is sprayed

commonErrors.error: Using a hose on dry solids before they are removed.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove solids by hand tools first, then rinse.

commonErrors.error: Using very hot water or steam for the first rinse.
commonErrors.prevention: Use cool or lukewarm water and let the site procedure set the temperature.

commonErrors.error: Spraying water onto motors or control panels.
commonErrors.prevention: Cover or isolate electrical equipment before the wet clean, and follow the site isolation procedure.

commonErrors.error: Leaving drains and channels out of the clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Include a drain check in every wet clean and record it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Food-area cleaning in Australia is regulated by state and territory food authorities and the Food Standards Code.
Wet floors and water running across walkways are slip hazards. Use warning signs and clear the walkway as the work moves.
Hot water and steam can scald. Do not use steam or hot-water cleaning unless trained and approved for the site.
Water and electricity do not mix. Do not direct water at motors, panels or outlets. The lesson does not cover electrical isolation, which must follow the site's own procedure.

qualityStandard: All solid debris is removed before any water is applied.
The rinse uses water at a temperature that does not set protein onto the surface.
No water reaches motors, control panels or outlets during the clean.
The drains are clear and water flows freely once the clean is finished.
documentationEvidence: Zones dry-cleared and rinsed, with start and finish times.
Any equipment that was disassembled, and any part that could not be cleaned.
Drain check result and any blockage reported.
summary: Remove solids by hand before any water is used.
Use cool or lukewarm rinse water; heat can set protein.
Keep water off electrical equipment and out of dry stores.
Clear the drains as part of every wet clean and record it.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should be removed first from a processing area?
options: Surface soil, using a high-pressure hose
Detergent, applied to the dry surface
Drains, once the floor has dried
Solid debris, using a shovel, scraper or broom

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is very hot water or steam avoided on food residue?
options: It can set protein onto the surface and make it harder to remove
It brightens stainless steel, so it is the preferred finish for the surface
It leaves a residue that cannot be rinsed away
It makes every detergent less effective

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should floor drains be cleaned as part of a wet clean?
options: Drains are only checked for water pressure and only when the floor looks wet
Soiled or blocked drains can become odour and contamination sources
Drains only need cleaning once a year and only if the floor smells
Drains do not need cleaning when the floor is dry and they can be ignored
